summary: This standards-track document adds a "keep" parameter to the SIP Via header so neighboring SIP entities can explicitly agree to use NAT keep-alive messages. It covers cases where SIP Outbound is unsupported, can't be used, or where keep-alive isn't otherwise negotiated. The keep-alives keep a NAT mapping open.

eli5.summary: A home router forgets connections that stay silent. This lets two phone systems agree to send little hello messages so the router remembers.

questions: how to keep nat bindings alive in sip
what is the sip via keep parameter
how often are sip keep-alives sent
subtitle: A Via header parameter that lets neighboring SIP devices agree to send NAT keep-alive messages.

tldr.problem: SIP Outbound can negotiate keep-alives only between a user agent and an edge proxy, and not when Outbound is unsupported, unusable or does not negotiate them implicitly.
tldr.mechanism: A new "keep" parameter on the Via header field lets adjacent SIP entities say they will send keep-alives, and the response can say they will receive them and how often.
tldr.outcome: Any two adjacent SIP entities can explicitly agree on keep-alives for a registration or a dialog, reusing the keep-alive mechanisms of SIP Outbound.

facts.label: Header parameter
facts.value: keep, on the Via header field

facts.label: Keep-alive spacing
facts.value: Randomly 80% to 100% of the recommended frequency

today: RFC 6223 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Keep-Alive Gap
sections.content:
Keep-alives are small messages sent so that a NAT keeps a binding open and requests can later travel back through it. SIP Outbound (RFC 5626) defines the keep-alive mechanisms, but it only lets a User Agent (UA) and an edge proxy negotiate them.

RFC 6223 defines a new Via header field parameter, keep, that lets adjacent SIP entities negotiate those same keep-alives explicitly. It lets an entity say it is willing to send keep-alives, say it is willing to receive them, and give a recommended frequency.
sections.eli5: A router that never hears from a friend forgets them. This is a way to agree to wave hello every so often.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC names three situations where explicit negotiation is needed:

  • Dialogs from non-registered UAs. A client that has not registered still needs its NAT binding kept open during a dialog. An emergency call is the typical example.
  • SIP Outbound not supported. Some entities support the keep-alive mechanisms without supporting Outbound.
  • Outbound flows started by a dialog. RFC 5626 does not implicitly negotiate keep-alives for such flows.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a phone has not signed in first, or does not know the older method. They still need a way to say let us keep in touch.

sections.title: How the Negotiation Works
sections.content:
A SIP entity that wants to send keep-alives inserts a keep parameter in the topmost Via header field it adds to a request. An entity that is willing to receive them adds a parameter value to keep in the response. When the sender sees a value in the response, it MUST start sending keep-alives to the same destination it would use for subsequent requests.

Negotiation is per direction, and the procedures are the same for UAs and proxies. The sender acts as a STUN client and the receiver as a STUN server, and both must also support the CRLF keep-alive from RFC 5626. Double-CRLF keep-alives are not forbidden even when nothing was negotiated, but keep tells the other side that they are supported.

An entity MUST NOT indicate willingness to send or receive keep-alives for a dialog unless it has inserted itself in the dialog route set. An ACK cannot carry keep, because it has no response. For an INVITE, at least one reliable response must carry the parameter value, and responses to the same request MUST NOT carry different values.
sections.eli5: One side asks, can I send you hello messages? The other side answers, yes, and here is how often. Each direction is asked separately.

sections.title: Registrations, Dialogs and Lifetime
sections.content:
For a registration, keep-alives are negotiated in a registration request, only from the registering entity towards the registrar. They last until the registration ends or a registration refresh is sent or forwarded. To continue, the entity MUST re-negotiate; otherwise it MUST stop sending them.

For a dialog, the negotiation uses an initial request or a mid-dialog target refresh request. Once negotiated, keep-alives MUST be sent for the dialog's lifetime and cannot be re-negotiated. A repeated keep on the same dialog towards the same neighbor MUST NOT be inserted, and is ignored if received.
sections.eli5: For a sign-in, you must ask again each time you renew it. For a phone call, you agree once and it lasts until you hang up.

sections.title: Keep-Alive Frequency
sections.content:
The value of keep in a response is a recommended keep-alive frequency in seconds. A non-zero value makes the receiver follow the Flow-Timer procedures of RFC 5626: send at least that often, and if using the recommended frequency, space keep-alives randomly between 80% and 100% of it. A value of zero means the sender can pick its own frequency.

If an entity also inserts a Flow-Timer header field in the same message, the two values MUST be identical. The keep parameter is more flexible because it works along the signalling path and can carry a different frequency per hop, which one Flow-Timer header cannot.
sections.eli5: The answer can include how often to say hello, such as every so many seconds. Zero means you pick.

sections.title: Grammar and Registration
sections.content:
The ABNF adds keep to the Via parameters: keep = "keep" [ EQUAL 1*(DIGIT) ]. The parameter alone is a request, and with a number it is an acceptance. IANA registered keep as a Via header field parameter with no predefined values.

The RFC does not define connection reuse. Entities wanting requests to flow back over the same connection need another mechanism, such as the alias parameter of RFC 5923 together with keep.
sections.eli5: The new word is simply keep, optionally followed by a number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unless SIP messages are integrity protected hop by hop, for example with TLS or DTLS, a man-in-the-middle can edit the Via fields. It could remove the keep-alive indications or set the timer very low, causing extra resource use.

A proxy MUST NOT put a value into keep in the topmost Via of a request it forwards, and SHOULD remove keep values from lower Via fields in responses. A malicious downstream entity could otherwise cause a proxy to receive STUN requests. So if STUN keep-alives get no response, the sender MUST stop sending them for the rest of the dialog or until re-negotiation for a registration.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky in the middle could change the agreement. So devices stop sending hello messages if nobody answers.
